newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore voters eyed economic perils in election.
newsitem.headline: Singapore voters eyed economic perils in election.

text.p: Singapore voters returned the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) by a landslide because personal well-being took priority over Western-style democratic principles, analysts and politicians said.

"When so much of a person's material well-being is tied to voting, you're asking for a lot of self-sacrifice," said Chua Beng Huat, a professor in the sociology department of the National University of Singapore.
At stake in Singapore's January 2 general election was a multi-billion dollar public housing renovation programme.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and PAP candidates had bluntly told voters, about 80 percent of whom live in public housing, they risked slipping to the end of the line for upgrading and other benefits if they voted for the opposition.
Goh later trumpeted the PAP sweep as a rejection by voters of the type of liberal democracy advocated by the West.
The PAP won 81 of the 83 seats at stake, the party's best general election result in 16 years. Goh also increased its popular vote to 65 percent from 61 percent.
"They have rejected Western-style liberal democracy and freedoms, putting individual rights over that of society," Goh told a post-victory news conference.
He said two leading opposition figures had tried and failed to "sell these Western agendas, promoted by the Western media and pressure groups like AsiaWatch", a human rights organisation.
Ministers also suggested the absence of a strong opposition here and stable politics was actually beneficial to Singapore.
Economic policies could be implemented rapidly and without huge delays, they said.

Observers, however, disagreed that the large swing in votes for the PAP in this election meant Singaporeans had shrugged off the significance of having a stronger opposition presence in parliament, checks and balances or greater accountability.
"(Just) because people have voted for self, does it mean they have given up wanting an alternative voice in government?" sociologist Chua asked.

Straits Times editor Leslie Fong wrote in a post-election editorial: "Pragmatism versus principle...at the end of a bitter campaign, which made many, many Singaporeans feel rather uncomfortable, the choice put before them was stark."
Analysts believe that victory was won on a mixture of Goh's personal popularity and hardball politics, but some opposition politicians claim voters were cowered into voting PAP.
"While they feel a need for an alternative voice in parliament, they feel they should not be the one (to vote them in), businessman and independent candidate, Chia Shi Teck, said.
"Right now people are obsessed with upgrading, these pocket issues," Chia said, noting in poll results those not threatened by upgrading were more willing to give him their support.
The overall bias toward material well-being was an outcome hard to avoid for any society, critics said.
"All these factors must have over-borne the judgement of voters when they came to cast their votes," chief of the Workers' Party Joshua Jeyaretnam told Reuters.
"(Goh's) words were either you take all or you take nothing. All means the whole package....I suppose one can't be too hard on them (voters)," Jeyaretnam added.
